table.text: The primary analyses were conducted in UK Biobank, a prospective cohort of approximately 500,000 participants recruited at 22 assessment centres across England, Scotland and Wales between 2006 and 2010.
Participants were aged 40 to 70 years at recruitment and provided questionnaire data, physical measurements and biological samples.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("P ≤ 5 × 10 -8", "P ≤ 5 × 10 -8", 
"P ≤ 10 -5", "P ≤ 0.05", "P ≤ 5 × 10 -8", "P ≤ 5 × 10 -8", 
"P > 0.01"), Text = c("QC-passing variants with P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 /6 were clumped using PLINK 63 (r² = 0.1; 500 kb).", 
"Sensitivity analyses used P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 ; traits with fewer than ten primary loci were additionally examined at P ≤ 10 -5 as exploratory analyses.", 
"Sensitivity analyses used P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 ; traits with fewer than ten primary loci were additionally examined at P ≤ 10 -5 as exploratory analyses.", 
"FUMA inputs were restricted to P ≤ 0.05, whereas MAGMA and SMR used the full eligible summary statistics.", 
"Sex-specific GWAS plots used P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 /12, accounting for six traits in each sex.", 
"European LD reference, an instrument QTL threshold of P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 and MAF ≥ 0.01.", 
"Support required SMR-multi q < 0.05 after global BH correction across all six traits and resources, together with HEIDI P > 0.01."
)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.formatted: Support required SMR-multi q < 0.05 after global BH correction across all six traits and resources, together with HEIDI P > 0.01.
table.expanded: Support required SMR-multi q < 0.05 after global BH correction across all six traits and resources, together with HEIDI P > 0.01.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P > 0.01", Sentence = "Support required SMR-multi q < 0.05 after global BH correction across all six traits and resources, together with HEIDI P > 0.01."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Biological aging clocks typically summarize complex biological profiles as a single age estimate, yet how uncertain these estimates are and whether this uncertainty represents a distinct, biologically meaningful dimension of human aging remain unclear.

Here, we develop a probabilistic framework across nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomic, plasma proteomic and routine blood test (RBT) profiles in more than 450,000 UK Biobank participants to derive biological age gap (BAG) and biological age uncertainty (BAU) from the mean and width of predicted-age distributions.
BAU was weakly correlated with BAG and increased with age-signal disagreement across individual molecules and organs, linking uncertainty to discordant aging across biological systems.

Higher BAU predicted mortality, loss of healthspan and multimorbidity independently of BAG, with mortality hazard ratios of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.23-1.26) and 1.40 (95% CI, 1.37-1.43) per standard deviation for NMR-and proteomic-derived BAU, respectively.

Adding BAU to conventional clinical models improved 10-year risk discrimination; moreover, longitudinal increases in NMR-derived BAU tracked subsequent health decline, and mortality associations were replicated using RBT-derived BAU across three independent external cohorts.
Multi-omics and physiological analyses linked BAU to inflammation, metabolic dysregulation and tissue remodeling beyond BAG.

Genetic analyses further revealed overlapping but distinct architectures of BAU and BAG, with BAU showing stronger genetic correlations with frailty and cardiometabolic diseases, and tissue and functional mapping implicating hepatic, immune and lipid-metabolic processes.

This study establishes a framework for characterizing biological age through both its mean deviation and uncertainty, defining BAU as an independent dimension of human aging that links discordant aging to future healthspan.
Aging is a heterogeneous process.
Individuals of the same chronological age differ substantially in physiological decline, molecular trajectories, and risks of aging-related disease and death [1] [2] [3] [4] .
text.formatted: Individuals of the same chronological age differ substantially in physiological decline, molecular trajectories, and risks of aging-related disease and death <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> .

text.text: Biological aging clocks made these differences quantifiable by estimating age from clinical, epigenetic and other molecular profiles [5] [6] [7] .
text.formatted: Biological aging clocks made these differences quantifiable by estimating age from clinical, epigenetic and other molecular profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> .

text.text: Organ-and system-specific clocks subsequently revealed distinct aging trajectories among organs and physiological systems within the same individual 1, 2, [8] [9] [10] .
text.formatted: Organ-and system-specific clocks subsequently revealed distinct aging trajectories among organs and physiological systems within the same individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> .

text.text: Recently, tissue-11 , cell-type- 12 , and transcriptomic clocks 13 have extended this resolution further.
text.formatted: Recently, tissue-11 , cell-type- <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> , and transcriptomic clocks <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> have extended this resolution further.

text.text: Therefore, aging can now be resolved across a nested hierarchy, from variation between individuals to variation among the organs, tissues, cell types, and molecular programs within them.
However, across this hierarchy, aging clocks typically summarize a multidimensional biological profile as a single estimated age 3, 14.
text.formatted: However, across this hierarchy, aging clocks typically summarize a multidimensional biological profile as a single estimated age <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: The difference between this single estimate and chronological age, termed the biological age gap (BAG), quantifies age deviation and is associated with healthspan, aging-related disease and mortality 3, 7, [15] [16] [17] .
text.formatted: The difference between this single estimate and chronological age, termed the biological age gap (BAG), quantifies age deviation and is associated with healthspan, aging-related disease and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> .

text.text: Nonetheless, biological age estimates carry predictive uncertainty, since a single biological profile often corresponds to a distribution of potential biological aging.
The breadth of this distribution indicates the precision of the estimate 14, 18 .
text.formatted: The breadth of this distribution indicates the precision of the estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: To make this uncertainty explicit, recent studies have applied individualized prediction intervals to epigenetic clocks during childhood development 19 .
text.formatted: To make this uncertainty explicit, recent studies have applied individualized prediction intervals to epigenetic clocks during childhood development <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Building on this observation, we define the width of an individual predictive age distribution as biological age uncertainty (BAU) and hypothesize that BAU represents a new dimension of biological aging, independent of BAG.
Biologically, this uncertainty reflects how consistently the signals within an individual profile support a common aging state.
Across physiological systems, aging progressively weakens functional coupling [20] [21] [22] , eroding the coordinated regulation required to preserve physiological integrity 23 .
text.formatted: Across physiological systems, aging progressively weakens functional coupling <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> , eroding the coordinated regulation required to preserve physiological integrity <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Intuitively, the divergence among aging signals captured by BAU can therefore serve as a proxy for discordant aging across biological systems.

Thus, it remains unclear whether BAU captures an independent dimension of human biological aging distinct from the age deviation quantified by BAG, and whether this uncertainty reflects discordant aging across biological systems and marks vulnerability to future health decline.
Here, we developed a probabilistic modelling framework that represents biological age as an individual predictive distribution, jointly characterizing age deviation and uncertainty.
Within . this framework, BAG and BAU are derived from the mean and width of the same distribution, respectively.
We applied this framework to large-scale nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomic and plasma proteomic profiles from UK Biobank.

We first evaluated whether BAU represents a dimension of biological aging distinct from BAG and whether higher BAU is associated with greater disagreement among molecular age signals and organ-specific BAGs.

We then examined whether baseline BAU and changes in BAU between assessments were associated with subsequent mortality, loss of healthspan, multimorbidity and incident diseases after accounting for BAG.
We also assessed whether adding BAU to conventional clinical risk models improved predictive discrimination.
To evaluate generalizability, we developed models based on routine blood tests (RBT) and evaluated the associations of RBT-derived BAU with mortality in three independent external cohorts.
We compared the molecular and pathway associations of BAU with those of BAG and examined whether these differences were reflected in physiological and clinical traits.

Finally, we characterized the genetic architectures of BAG and BAU, examined their genetic correlations with aging-related traits, and used tissue and functional mapping to identify associated tissues, cell types and biological pathways.

Taken together, these analyses demonstrate that biological aging can be characterized by both mean age deviation and uncertainty in the age estimate, with greater uncertainty potentially reflecting more discordant aging across biological systems.

We developed a probabilistic modelling framework to derive BAG and BAU, with a mathematical formulation providing a theoretical interpretation of these measures in terms of mean aging and discordant aging across biological subsystems (Fig. 1a, Methods, and Supplementary Notes 1-4).
text.formatted: We developed a probabilistic modelling framework to derive BAG and BAU, with a mathematical formulation providing a theoretical interpretation of these measures in terms of mean aging and discordant aging across biological subsystems (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1a</ref>, Methods, and Supplementary Notes 1-4).

text.text: Separate NMR and proteomic age models were trained and independently calibrated in healthy reference participants, then applied to participants in held-out assessment centres.
This yielded predicted-age distributions for 272,672 participants with NMR measurements and 43,867 with proteomic measurements (Extended Data Fig. 1).
text.formatted: This yielded predicted-age distributions for 272,672 participants with NMR measurements and 43,867 with proteomic measurements (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1</ref>).

text.text: BAG represented the deviation of mean predicted age from chronological age, whereas BAU represented the width of the predicted-age distribution (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: BAG represented the deviation of mean predicted age from chronological age, whereas BAU represented the width of the predicted-age distribution (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1b</ref>).

text.text: Both measures were derived from calibrated predictions, with BAU calculated from log predictive variance, and were adjusted for age and standardized within sex relative to healthy reference participants.
We first examined whether BAU distinguished individuals with similar BAG.
Participants matched for age, sex and NMR-derived BAG had predicted-age distributions with similar means but different widths (Fig. 1c).
text.formatted: Participants matched for age, sex and NMR-derived BAG had predicted-age distributions with similar means but different widths (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1c</ref>).

text.text: Across the study populations, BAG and BAU were weakly correlated for both NMR-derived measures (Pearson r = -0.07) and proteomics-derived measures (r = 0.18; Fig. 1d).
text.formatted: Across the study populations, BAG and BAU were weakly correlated for both NMR-derived measures (Pearson r = -0.07) and proteomics-derived measures (r = 0.18; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1d</ref>).

text.text: These observations indicate that BAG and BAU captured distinct aspects of the predicted age distribution.
Individual molecular measurements within the same person can support different ages when compared with healthy reference profiles.
We therefore examined whether greater disagreement among these molecular age signals was associated with higher BAU.
Using healthy reference profiles, we identified the age that best fitted each participant's molecular measurements collectively.

For each molecule, we calculated the difference in log-likelihood between its individually best-fitting age and this common age, then averaged these differences to quantify molecular age-signal disagreement (Extended Data Fig. 2a).

text.text: Among participants with similar BAG, greater protein age-signal disagreement accompanied higher proteomic-derived BAU (Fig. 1e).

text.text: Across both assays, greater molecular age-signal disagreement was associated with higher BAU after adjustment for BAG and demographic and assay covariates (Fig. 1f,g).

text.text: We next tested whether this relationship extended to differences in age estimates across . organs.
We quantified organ-age disagreement as the within-participant SD of ten proteomic-derived organ BAGs (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

We further evaluated whether BAU was consistent over time, whether measured potential confounders explained its variation, and whether its estimates depended on algorithm choice.

After subtracting these models' predictions, the remaining BAU was strongly correlated with original BAU (Spearman r = 0.843 and 0.854, respectively), indicating that the measured factors accounted for a limited proportion of BAU variation and that higher BAU remained evident after adjustment (Extended Data Fig. 2e).

text.text: Together, these findings support the consistency of BAU over time and across algorithms, with its variation not primarily explained by measured potential confounders.
Collectively, these results characterize BAU as a robust phenotype distinct from the mean age deviation measured by BAG.
Higher BAU reflects a broader predicted-age distribution and is associated with greater disagreement among molecular and organ age signals.
We next examined whether BAU stratified future health risk beyond BAG.
Participants were classified into four groups defined by low or high BAG and BAU, using zero on the healthy-reference scale as the threshold.

Over 15 years, participants with high BAU had higher cumulative probabilities of all-cause mortality, loss of healthspan and major disease multimorbidity within both low and high BAG groups in both proteomic-and NMR-based models (Fig. 2a,c).

text.text: We then assessed whether BAU improved risk discrimination when added to conventional clinical factors.

In held-out assessment centres, adding BAU to the baseline clinical model increased the 10-year C-index by 0.002 to 0.005 for NMR and 0.011 to 0.022 for proteomics across the three primary outcomes, respectively.
Models combining both BAG and BAU achieved the largest improvement for each outcome, with increments of 0.003 to 0.007 for NMR and 0.017 to 0.039 for proteomics (Fig. 2e).

text.text: Longitudinal changes in BAU also carried information about subsequent health.
Among 13,620 participants with repeat NMR measurements, we assessed whether BAU change between reassessment and baseline was associated with health outcomes.

Each 1 SD higher BAU change was associated with subsequent mortality (HR, 1.283; 95% CI, 1.176 to 1.399), loss of healthspan (HR, 1.187; 1.121 to 1.258) and multimorbidity (HR, 1.448; 1.324 to 1.583), after accounting for baseline BAG and BAU, BAG change and demographic, behavioural and socioeconomic covariates (Fig. 2f).

text.text: Sensitivity analyses supported the prospective associations of BAG and BAU.
In both assays, associations with all 12 outcomes remained positive after extended covariate adjustment and exclusion of events during the first year of follow-up.

text.text: Altogether, these findings support BAU as an independent indicator of future health risk beyond BAG.

Associations with adverse health outcomes were consistent across NMR-derived, proteomic-derived and RBT-derived BAU, supported by subgroup analyses and replication of mortality associations in three external cohorts.
Longitudinal changes in NMR-derived BAU were also associated with subsequent risk after accounting for baseline BAG and BAU.
Adding BAU to conventional clinical prediction models improved risk discrimination, with models combining BAG and BAU achieving the greatest improvement.
We next examined the molecular correlates of BAU using cross-omic analyses, relating NMR-derived BAU to plasma proteins and proteomic-derived BAU to NMR measures.
This analysis assessed associations in a different omic layer from the features used to derive BAU, with BAG and BAU included together in each model.
Higher NMR-derived BAU was associated with higher levels of the stress-responsive cytokine GDF15 and complement receptor VSIG4, and lower APOM and PON3 (Fig. 3a).

text.text: These associations were replicated in held-out assessment centres, linking BAU to reproducible differences in proteins involved in stress responses and immunity, alongside glucose and lipoprotein measures.
We then compared the molecular associations of BAU with those of BAG to determine whether the two measures captured similar or distinct molecular profiles.
Their association estimates were correlated across proteins (r = 0.523) and NMR measures (r = 0.302), but . differed in both magnitude and direction (Fig. 3c).

text.text: Glucose and albumin showed larger absolute association coefficients for proteomic-derived BAU, whereas creatinine showed a larger coefficient for proteomic-derived BAG.
APOM and FGFBP1 had positive coefficients for NMR-derived BAG and negative coefficients for NMR-derived BAU.
These comparisons indicate that BAU and BAG share some molecular correlates while showing distinct associations with specific proteins and metabolic measures.
To interpret these molecular differences, we compared protein pathway enrichment for BAG, BAU and their coefficient contrast.

Both measures were associated with IL-6-JAK-STAT3 signalling and inflammatory response pathways, whereas interleukin-10 signalling and neutrophil degranulation showed more positive associations with BAU than with BAG.

In the NMR model, NMR-derived BAU showed negative associations with NR1H2/NR1H3 signalling and extracellular matrix proteoglycan pathways, whereas NMR-derived BAG showed more positive associations with coagulation and lipoprotein remodelling.

In the proteomic model, proteomic-derived BAU was associated with collagen degradation, and coefficient comparisons identified differences involving fatty acid metabolism, myogenesis and extracellular matrix pathways (Fig. 3d).

text.text: Gene Ontology analyses further supported these functional differences through enrichment of immune, granule, lipoprotein and extracellular matrix processes (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b).

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that BAU and BAG share inflammatory associations but differ in their associations with immune regulation, lipid metabolism and tissue remodelling.
We next assessed whether these molecular differences were reflected in independently measured physiological traits.

Across 28 traits, both NMR-derived and proteomic-derived BAU showed stronger positive associations than the corresponding BAG measures with C-reactive protein, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, body mass index and waist-to-hip ratio.
Proteomic-derived BAG showed stronger associations with cystatin C and urea (Fig. 3e).

text.text: The associations with inflammatory and adiposity-related traits provided physiological counterparts to the molecular findings, while the renal function markers further distinguished the correlates of BAG and BAU.
We performed sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the molecular findings.

Association patterns remained largely consistent after additional adjustment for absolute BAG, allowing nonlinear associations with BAG, excluding extreme BAG values or restricting . analyses to participants with low assay missingness.

Among participants healthy at baseline, molecular associations generally retained their direction, although their magnitudes were attenuated, and some pathway differences were attenuated (Extended Data Fig. 6c-e).

text.text: These results support the robustness of the molecular findings across modelling choices and sample restrictions, with the primary association patterns also evident in participants healthy at baseline.
To sum up, these findings distinguish the molecular and physiological correlates of BAU from those of BAG.
BAU showed prominent associations with immune, metabolic and tissue-remodelling processes, together with physiological markers of inflammation and adiposity.
Differences from BAG extended across molecular association strength and direction, pathway enrichment and clinical traits.

RBT-derived BAG showed enrichment for retinoic acid and xenobiotic metabolism, whereas NMR-derived BAG was enriched for phospholipid homeostasis and fatty acid degradation.
Both BAU traits showed enrichment for positive regulation of sterol transport, with CETP, LIPG and NR1H3 contributing to this . shared enrichment.
Whereas CETP and LIPG were prioritized across all four traits, NR1H3 was prioritized for both BAU traits but neither BAG trait.
The shared 11p11.2 locus containing NR1H3 was represented by rs35184771 in RBT-derived BAU (P = 1.54 × 10 -16 ) and rs113253936 in NMR-derived BAU (P = 1.24 × 10 -10 ).
NR1H3 encodes LXR α, linking these findings to the established role of LXR signaling in coordinating lipid metabolism and macrophage inflammatory responses 35 .
text.formatted: NR1H3 encodes LXR α, linking these findings to the established role of LXR signaling in coordinating lipid metabolism and macrophage inflammatory responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> .

text.text: Additionally, RBT-derived BAU showed enrichment for T-cell receptor signaling.
The immune-related profile of RBT-derived BAU was further supported by DisGeNET enrichment for gene sets associated with asthma and systemic lupus erythematosus.
These representative enrichment patterns were retained under alternative gene-background and prioritization criteria (Supplementary Table 23).
text.formatted: These representative enrichment patterns were retained under alternative gene-background and prioritization criteria (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">23</ref>).

text.text: Together, these analyses highlighted differing enrichment profiles within a shared lipid-metabolic background, with additional links to immune-inflammatory processes particularly evident for BAU.
Our study introduces a probabilistic framework for characterizing biological age through both mean age deviation and uncertainty, quantified by BAG and BAU, respectively.

Within this framework, individuals with similar BAG differed substantially in BAU, with greater BAU associated with more discordant aging, reflected in molecular age-signal disagreement and organ-age disagreement.
Higher BAU was associated with mortality, loss of healthspan and multimorbidity beyond BAG, while incorporating both measures improved clinical risk discrimination.
Associations with subsequent health decline were also evident for longitudinal increases in BAU, and RBT-derived BAU showed mortality associations in three independent external cohorts.
Cross-omic and genetic analyses revealed distinct molecular profiles and genetic architectures for BAU and BAG, with BAU showing prominent links to immune and metabolic regulation.

Collectively, these findings establish BAU as a biologically informative dimension of human aging and show how a distributional representation of biological age can connect variation in the coherence of aging signals to differences in future health vulnerability.
Our findings show that a probabilistic representation of biological age contains two distinct dimensions.

Although aging clocks have progressively expanded from predicting chronological age 15 to capturing multisystem physiological state 36, 37 , mortality risk 38 , longitudinal pace of aging 39 and organ-specific molecular changes 1, 8 , each modeled aspect remains typically represented by a single scalar estimate 40 .
text.formatted: Although aging clocks have progressively expanded from predicting chronological age <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> to capturing multisystem physiological state <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> , mortality risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> , longitudinal pace of aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> and organ-specific molecular changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , each modeled aspect remains typically represented by a single scalar estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> .

text.text: For age prediction models, this scalar locates an individual along an aging axis, making BAG the primary phenotype of interindividual variation.
In our probabilistic framework, BAG describes the deviation of mean predicted age from chronological age, whereas BAU characterizes the width of the predicted-age distribution.
Individuals with similar mean predicted ages can therefore differ in the uncertainty associated with those estimates.

Consistent with this distinction, participants with closely matched BAG exhibited markedly different BAU (Fig. 1c), and the two measures were weakly correlated in both the NMR and proteomic models (Fig. 1d).
text.formatted: Consistent with this distinction, participants with closely matched BAG exhibited markedly different BAU (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1c</ref>), and the two measures were weakly correlated in both the NMR and proteomic models (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1d</ref>).

text.text: Considering both the mean and width of the age distribution provides a two-dimensional framework for characterizing individual differences in biological aging.
The clinical value of BAU lies in how it transforms the health-related interpretation of BAG.
Previous studies have established BAG as the principal metric linking biological clocks to mortality and aging-related diseases 1, 3, 9 , while individual uncertainty has conventionally been.
text.formatted: Previous studies have established BAG as the principal metric linking biological clocks to mortality and aging-related diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> , while individual uncertainty has conventionally been.

text.text: treated as a measure of statistical precision or evidential strength 18, 19 .
text.formatted: treated as a measure of statistical precision or evidential strength <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Our findings demonstrate that this uncertainty arises not only from statistical uncertainty but also from underlying discordant aging process, with biological relevance, such as directly reflecting clinical vulnerability.

Across both low-and high-BAG strata, individuals with high BAU exhibited elevated 15-year risks of mortality, loss of healthspan, and multimorbidity (Fig. 2a,c), maintaining independent predictive value after adjusting for BAG and established clinical risk factors (Fig. 2b,d).
text.formatted: Across both low-and high-BAG strata, individuals with high BAU exhibited elevated 15-year risks of mortality, loss of healthspan, and multimorbidity (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_15">2a</ref>,<ref type="figure">c</ref>), maintaining independent predictive value after adjusting for BAG and established clinical risk factors (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_15">2b</ref>,<ref type="figure">d</ref>).

text.text: High BAU can thus uncover hidden susceptibility even among individuals classified as biologically young by BAG alone.
Furthermore, combining BAG and BAU achieved improved risk prediction across outcomes, with longitudinal increases in BAU offering additional predictive value for future health decline.

Evaluating BAU alongside BAG thus differentiates individuals with similar estimated biological age but diverging health risk, establishing both the location and uncertainty of an age distribution as essential components of biological aging assessment and risk stratification.
The associations of BAU with molecular age-signal disagreement and organ-age disagreement link uncertainty to discordant aging across biological systems.

Higher NMR-derived and proteomics-derived BAU were associated with greater disagreement among molecular age signals within their respective assays (Fig. 1f-g), and higher proteomic-derived BAU was also associated with greater disagreement among organ-specific BAGs (Fig. 1h).
text.formatted: Higher NMR-derived and proteomics-derived BAU were associated with greater disagreement among molecular age signals within their respective assays (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1f-g</ref>), and higher proteomic-derived BAU was also associated with greater disagreement among organ-specific BAGs (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">1h</ref>).

text.text: These associations suggest that BAU reflects differences in the alignment of aging-related signals within an individual.

Our mathematical framework provides a theoretical perspective for this interpretation by linking divergence among subsystem aging states to a broader predicted-age distribution and increased risk of adverse health outcomes at a given mean aging level.
Discordant aging across biological systems, reflected by higher BAU, thus offers a distinct perspective on biological aging alongside the mean age deviation measured by BAG.
Empirical observations across biological scales further support the biological relevance of coordinated function.
Aged cardiomyocytes exhibit heightened cell-to-cell variability in gene expression 20 , and advanced age impairs coordinated transcriptional responses to immune challenge 21 .
text.formatted: Aged cardiomyocytes exhibit heightened cell-to-cell variability in gene expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> , and advanced age impairs coordinated transcriptional responses to immune challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Furthermore, homeostatic dysregulation accumulates along partially independent physiological axes, predicting frailty, chronic disease, and mortality 22 , while physiological resilience depends on coordinated multi-system responses to restore homeostasis following perturbation 23 .
text.formatted: Furthermore, homeostatic dysregulation accumulates along partially independent physiological axes, predicting frailty, chronic disease, and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> , while physiological resilience depends on coordinated multi-system responses to restore homeostasis following perturbation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Collectively, these theoretical and empirical insights provide a biological rationale for the predictive value of BAU.
The molecular divergence between BAU and BAG indicates that they capture distinct layers of biological aging.

While BAG was predominantly linked to lipoprotein transport, tissue structure, and organ function, reflecting accumulated shifts in steady-state physiological capacity 41 , BAU was associated with interconnected components of the systemic stress response, including inflammatory activation, metabolic adjustment, and tissue remodeling.
text.formatted: While BAG was predominantly linked to lipoprotein transport, tissue structure, and organ function, reflecting accumulated shifts in steady-state physiological capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> , BAU was associated with interconnected components of the systemic stress response, including inflammatory activation, metabolic adjustment, and tissue remodeling.

text.text: Among signals associated with BAU, GDF15 is induced by the integrated stress response during nutritional and cellular stress 42 and contributes to the control of aging-related inflammation and metabolic homeostasis 43 , whereas higher glycoprotein acetyls provide a complementary signal of persistent inflammation and neutrophil activity 44 .
text.formatted: Among signals associated with BAU, GDF15 is induced by the integrated stress response during nutritional and cellular stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> and contributes to the control of aging-related inflammation and metabolic homeostasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> , whereas higher glycoprotein acetyls provide a complementary signal of persistent inflammation and neutrophil activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> .

text.text: Experimental evidence directly links these pathways, as NLRP3-mediated sterile inflammation impairs metabolic control during aging 45 , and senescent cell secretomes concurrently release GDF15 alongside matrix-remodeling proteases 46 .
text.formatted: Experimental evidence directly links these pathways, as NLRP3-mediated sterile inflammation impairs metabolic control during aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> , and senescent cell secretomes concurrently release GDF15 alongside matrix-remodeling proteases <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> .

text.text: The simultaneous enrichment of these pathways in high BAU profiles depicts a systemic state in which stress sensing, metabolic adaptation, and tissue repair are chronically engaged.

Differential activation of these pathways across biological systems may contribute to discordant aging, reflected in disagreement among age-informative signals, consistent with the progressive homeostatic dysregulation and heightened biological heterogeneity characteristic of aging 22, 47 .
text.formatted: Differential activation of these pathways across biological systems may contribute to discordant aging, reflected in disagreement among age-informative signals, consistent with the progressive homeostatic dysregulation and heightened biological heterogeneity characteristic of aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> .

text.text: In this view, BAG quantifies the magnitude of accumulated molecular and functional change, whereas BAU captures discordant aging across biological systems related to systemic regulatory instability.
Genetic analyses extend these molecular findings by revealing distinct health-related associations and functional enrichment profiles for BAG and BAU.
Within RBT-and NMR-derived traits, negative BAG-BAU genetic correlations and opposing associations at shared variants argue against treating the two phenotypes as interchangeable measures of aging.
BAU showed higher positive genetic correlation estimates than BAG for aging-related phenotypes related to inflammation, frailty and metabolic dysfunction.
Key associations persisted after adjustment for BAG, supporting health-related genetic information not fully captured by BAG.

The positive genetic correlation of NMR-derived BAU with HD Biological Age 30 is consistent with BAU capturing aspects of physiological dysregulation and suggests that the uncertainty it quantifies may have biological relevance in aging-related biomarker patterns.
Functional mapping places these differences within metabolic systems shared by both phenotypes.
Common lipid-pathway enrichment can involve different genes and cellular contexts, allowing BAG and BAU to reflect different aspects of interconnected biological processes.
The additional immune-related enrichment observed for BAU provides a . functional context for its genetic associations with inflammation and frailty.
The prioritization of NR1H3, encoding LXRα, in both BAU traits offers a relevant connection to established biology.

Predictive variances were then rescaled using prediction errors obtained from cross-fitted mean calibration within the same healthy calibration set: where C s denotes the sex-specific healthy calibration set and m i cf denotes the corresponding cross-fitted calibrated mean.
This rescaling aligned the magnitude of the predicted variances with the observed squared prediction errors in the healthy calibration set.
Raw biological age gap and uncertainty were defined as: where log denotes the natural logarithm.
To remove residual age dependence, we fitted sex-specific LOWESS curves for calibrated age gap and log predictive variance as functions of chronological age in the healthy calibration set.

BAG and BAU were calculated by subtracting the corresponding fitted age trends and dividing by the residual standard deviations in that set: where τ g,s and τ u,s denote the sex-specific residual standard deviations in the healthy calibration set.

Positive BAG therefore indicates a higher mean predicted age than expected for a healthy participant of the same chronological age and sex, whereas positive BAU indicates greater uncertainty than expected on the same reference scale.
Calibration and reference parameters were estimated in each fold's healthy calibration set and applied unchanged to participants in the held-out centres.

BAG and BAU at reassessment were calculated using the same age models, preprocessing parameters, calibration functions and healthy-reference parameters used at baseline.
Spearman correlations between baseline and reassessment values were calculated for both measures to compare their consistency over time.
To assess how much BAU variation was explained by potential confounders, we fitted auxiliary LightGBM regression models with BAU as the outcome.
Models were fitted in four assessment-centre folds and evaluated in the fifth, yielding one out-of-fold prediction per participant.

We examined whether higher BAU, which indicates a broader predicted-age distribution, was associated with greater disagreement among age signals within an individual.
At the molecular level, we assessed how well a common age could describe a participant's protein or NMR measurements.
At the organ level, we quantified differences among organ-specific BAGs.
We then examined the associations of these disagreement measures with BAU after adjustment for overall BAG.
Molecular disagreement was calculated separately using the 204 protein inputs and 168 NMR measures of the corresponding age models.
For each molecular measure, we first estimated how its expected level varied with age in healthy participants.
Within each outer fold, . sex-specific reference curves were fitted using natural cubic splines of age with four degrees of freedom in the healthy model-fitting set.
The independent healthy calibration set was then used to correct the mean residual and estimate the residual standard deviation.

These reference curves and residual standard deviations were used to calculate the likelihood of each held-out participant's observed measurements across candidate ages from 40 to 70 years at 0.25-year intervals.

For participant i , we calculated the Gaussian log-likelihood of each observed molecular measurement x ij at candidate age a as where j indexes molecular measures, μ j a is the expected level of measure j at age a after calibration, and σ j is its residual standard deviation in the healthy calibration set.
Both quantities were estimated separately by sex and outer fold.
Age-independent constants were omitted because they cancel when calculating molecular disagreement.
For each participant, we identified the age that maximized the log-likelihood of each molecular measurement separately.
We also identified a common support age a i * that maximized the mean log-likelihood across all observed measurements.

Molecular disagreement was defined as the mean reduction in log-likelihood when each measurement was evaluated at this common support age rather than its individually best-fitting age, where � i contains the indices of the molecular measures observed for participant i, and � i is their number.

Larger values indicate that a common support age provides a poorer fit relative to allowing each molecular measure its own best-fitting age, reflecting greater disagreement among molecular age signals.
The calculation used only observed measurements.
Organ-age disagreement quantified the variation in organ-specific BAGs within each participant.

Within each outer fold, predicted organ ages were calibrated by regressing chronological age on predicted age in the healthy calibration set, separately by sex.
For each organ, we then calculated the difference between calibrated predicted age and chronological age.
Its association with chronological age was fitted using a natural cubic spline with four degrees of freedom in the same calibration set.
The fitted age-dependent mean was subtracted from each participant's organ age gap, and the result was divided by the calibration residual standard deviation to obtain organ-specific BAG.

For participants with all ten organ BAGs available, organ-age disagreement was defined as D i org = 1 10 k=1 10 BAG ik -BAG i 2 , where BAG ik is the standardized BAG for organ k in participant i , and BAG i is that participant's mean BAG across the ten organs.
Larger values indicate greater differences in BAG among organs.

Baseline hazards were stratified by baseline assessment centre.
Outcome definitions and censoring followed those described for the baseline analyses.
Hazard ratios were reported per 1 SD increase in BAG or BAU change, with 95% confidence intervals calculated using model-based standard errors.
To examine whether BAU derived from routinely available blood measurements was associated with future health risk, we developed a probabilistic age model in UK Biobank.
Model development followed the same five centre-based outer folds, healthy-reference selection, calibration and BAG and BAU derivation procedures as the NMR and proteomic . models.
Associations of RBT-derived BAG and BAU with the three primary outcomes and nine incident diseases were evaluated using the prospective survival models described above.
For external validation, we trained separate models in healthy UK Biobank participants using the blood measurements available in each external cohort.
The panels comprised 24 measurements for NHANES, 16 for CHARLS and 18 for CHNS (Supplementary Table 34).
text.formatted: The panels comprised 24 measurements for NHANES, 16 for CHARLS and 18 for CHNS (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">34</ref>).

text.text: Preprocessing parameters and fitted age models were estimated in UK Biobank, with calibration based on an independent healthy calibration set.
These parameters and models were applied unchanged to the corresponding external cohort.
BAG and BAU were calculated using the age-and sex-specific healthy references established in UK Biobank.
Mortality analyses included 24,225 participants in NHANES, 9,604 in CHARLS and 5,137 in CHNS.
Cox proportional hazards models included BAG and BAU simultaneously and adjusted for the demographic, behavioural and health covariates specified for each cohort (Supplementary Table 30).
text.formatted: Cox proportional hazards models included BAG and BAU simultaneously and adjusted for the demographic, behavioural and health covariates specified for each cohort (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">30</ref>).

text.text: Hazard ratios were reported per 1 SD increase on the corresponding UK Biobank healthy-reference scale.
NHANES mortality was obtained through linkage to the National Death Index.
For CHARLS and CHNS, deaths recorded between survey waves were assigned to the midpoint of the corresponding interval.
Sensitivity analyses used the earliest and latest plausible death dates within each interval (Supplementary Table 35).
text.formatted: Sensitivity analyses used the earliest and latest plausible death dates within each interval (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">35</ref>).

text.text: We performed separate sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the prospective associations of BAG and BAU.
Extended adjustment added diet, medication use, family history, body mass index, systolic blood pressure and baseline disease burden to the primary models.
A one-year landmark analysis began follow-up one year after baseline among participants who remained alive, under observation and free of the target outcome.
To examine associations across follow-up periods, we fitted separate models for 0-5, 5-10 and more than 10 years, including participants still at risk at the start of each interval.
Fine-Gray models accounted for death as a competing event for multimorbidity and the nine nonfatal disease outcomes.
We also repeated the outcome analyses using BAG and BAU derived from LightGBMLSS and XGBoostLSS, retaining the same outcome definitions and covariate adjustment.

We examined whether associations with the three primary outcomes differed by age, sex, baseline health status, body mass index, current smoking and physical activity, separately for NMR-derived and proteomic-derived measures.
Each Cox model included BAG, BAU, the subgroup variable and its interactions with both BAG and BAU, with adjustment following the primary analyses.
Subgroup-specific hazard ratios were estimated from these models.
Differences between subgroups were assessed using global Wald tests of the interaction terms for BAG and BAU separately, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the interaction tests.
We examined whether BAU and BAG were associated with different molecular profiles.
For NMR-derived BAG and BAU, we analysed associations with 2,919 plasma proteins.
For proteomic-derived BAG and BAU, we analysed associations with 168 NMR measures.
Assessment-centre folds 1-3 formed the discovery set, and folds 4-5 formed the validation set.

Molecular measurements below the 0.5th or above the 99.5th percentile were set to the corresponding percentile values, then standardized using means and standard deviations from healthy participants in the discovery set.
All preprocessing parameters were determined in the discovery set and applied unchanged to the validation set.
Each protein or NMR measure was analysed among participants with an observed value for that measure.
For each molecular outcome, we fitted a linear regression model containing both BAG and BAU to estimate their mutually adjusted associations.
Models also included chronological age, sex, ethnicity, assessment centre, attendance date, season and the proportion of missing measurements in the outcome assay.
Chronological age was modelled using a natural cubic spline with four degrees of freedom, and standard errors were clustered by assessment centre.
Associations were tested two-sided in the discovery set, with the FDR controlled at 5%.
Associations meeting this threshold were tested one-sided in the validation set in the direction observed in the discovery set.
Replication required the same association direction and an FDR below 5% in the validation set.
To compare the molecular associations of BAG and BAU, we plotted their coefficients estimated in the discovery set from the same joint model for all proteins and NMR measures (Fig. 3c).
text.formatted: To compare the molecular associations of BAG and BAU, we plotted their coefficients estimated in the discovery set from the same joint model for all proteins and NMR measures (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">3c</ref>).

text.text: Coefficient signs indicated association direction, and the continuous colour scale represented the difference in absolute coefficient magnitude, M = β BAU -β BAG .
We also formally tested the signed coefficient difference, Δ = β BAU -β BAG , using a standard error that accounted for the covariance between the two estimates.
These differences were evaluated using the same criteria in the discovery and validation sets as the individual associations.
To interpret the biological processes associated with BAG and BAU, we performed pathway analyses using their protein associations.
For the NMR age model, we used associations with all 2,919 proteins.
For the proteomic age model, we analysed associations with the 2,715 proteins remaining after exclusion of the 204 model inputs, using the same joint regression framework.
Proteins were ranked separately for BAG, BAU and the signed difference between their coefficients.
Each ranking statistic was calculated by dividing the coefficient, or coefficient difference, by its standard error.
Gene-set enrichment analysis used the complete ranked protein lists and the Hallmark and Reactome collections from MSigDB 2026.1.
Hs.
Gene sets containing 10-500 measured proteins were retained.
In the discovery set, FDR was controlled separately for each ranking and collection.
Pathways meeting an FDR below 5% in the discovery set were evaluated in the validation set, with FDR controlled within the corresponding selected pathway set.
Replication required enrichment in the same direction and an FDR below 5% in the validation set.
We also used Gene Ontology over-representation analysis to identify functions enriched among proteins with replicated associations.
Separate protein sets were defined by positive and negative associations with BAG, positive and negative associations with BAU, and positive and negative BAU-minus-BAG coefficient differences.
Each set was examined for enrichment in biological processes, cellular components and molecular functions, using the eligible measured proteins mapped to each category as the background.
Enrichment was assessed using one-sided hypergeometric tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction applied separately within each protein set and Gene Ontology category.
Sensitivity analyses assessed whether the molecular findings were robust to alternative ways of accounting for BAG, restrictions on assay missingness and baseline health status.

We repeated the analyses after separately adding absolute BAG to the model, modelling BAG using a natural cubic spline, restricting participants to the central 95% of BAG, restricting participants to those with low missingness in the outcome assay, or restricting participants to.
those healthy at baseline.
BAU association coefficients were compared with those from the primary analysis.
Pathway analyses were also repeated among participants healthy at baseline, using the same enrichment and validation procedures.

To examine whether the molecular differences between BAG and BAU were reflected at the physiological level, we analysed their associations with 28 physiological and clinical traits (Supplementary Table 36).
text.formatted: To examine whether the molecular differences between BAG and BAU were reflected at the physiological level, we analysed their associations with 28 physiological and clinical traits (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">36</ref>).

text.text: Traits directly overlapping with NMR age-model inputs were excluded.
The discovery and validation sets followed the same assessment-centre folds as the molecular analyses.
Trait measurements were winsorized, transformed where appropriate and standardized relative to healthy participants in the discovery set.
The same preprocessing parameters were applied to the validation set.
Each trait was analysed using a linear regression model containing BAG and BAU simultaneously.

Models adjusted for chronological age using a natural cubic spline with four degrees of freedom, sex, ethnicity, current smoking, alcohol intake, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, education, household income, employment status, assessment centre, attendance date, season and the proportion of missing measurements among the corresponding age-model inputs.
Standard errors were clustered by assessment centre.
Differences between BAG and BAU coefficients were tested while accounting for their covariance within the same model.
Associations and coefficient differences were evaluated using the same discovery and validation criteria as the molecular analyses.
We analyzed BAG and BAU derived from RBT, NMR metabolomics and plasma proteomics.
Calibrated, standardized phenotypes were linked to genetic covariates by participant identifier.
Analyses included participants of European ancestry whose recorded sex matched their genetically inferred sex and who had complete data for all covariates.

The analysis samples comprised 173,318 males and 203,275 females for RBT-derived traits, 105,521 males and 123,572 females for NMR-derived traits, and 16,571 males and 19,467 females for proteomics-derived traits, respectively.
Participants could contribute to more than one biomarker source.
GWASs used the calibrated, age-adjusted and standardized BAG and BAU measures described above.
No additional standardization or rank-based inverse-normal transformation was applied during GWAS preparation.
Pooled-sample GWASs used the same framework with an additional sex covariate.
These pooled analyses were reported separately from the cross-sex meta-analyses, which supplied the primary downstream summary statistics.
Male and female GWASs were combined by fixed-effect inverse-variance meta-analysis using the STDERR scheme in METAL (release 5 May 2020), with genomic control disabled 56.

Genomic loci were defined using FUMA SNP2GENE (v1.8.2) 57 with GRCh37 coordinates and the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 European reference panel 58 .
text.formatted: Genomic loci were defined using FUMA SNP2GENE (v1.8.2) <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> with GRCh37 coordinates and the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 European reference panel <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> .

text.text: The executed FUMA configuration used a significance threshold of 8.3 × 10 -9 , linkage disequilibrium (LD) thresholds of r² = 0.6 and 0.1 for independent significant and lead single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), respectively, and a 250-kb within-trait locus-merging distance.
Reference-panel variants were included with a reference MAF threshold of zero; uploaded variants remained subject to MAF ≥ 0.01.
Loci overlapping the extended major histocompatibility complex (MHC; chromosome 6:28,477,797-33,448,354) were excluded from reported counts.
Unique loci across the six traits were obtained by merging same-chromosome FUMA intervals overlapping by at least one base pair, including transitive overlaps, without additional flanking distance.
Each merged locus was represented by the constituent FUMA top lead SNP with the smallest P value; ties were resolved by a fixed trait order, position and rsID.
Cytogenetic bands were assigned using the UCSC hg19 cytoBand annotation.
Within each biomarker source, locus sharing was expressed as the proportion of BAU loci overlapping a BAG locus.
Regional comparisons used each trait's smallest available P value within the merged interval, retaining missing results as missing.
Shared significant variants were matched by position and unordered allele pair, and selected effect-direction comparisons were aligned to the same effect allele.
Observed-scale SNP heritability was estimated using univariate LD score regression (LDSC v1.0.1) for the sex-specific, cross-sex meta-analysis and pooled-sample GWASs 59 .
text.formatted: Observed-scale SNP heritability was estimated using univariate LD score regression (LDSC v1.0.1) for the sex-specific, cross-sex meta-analysis and pooled-sample GWASs <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> .

text.text: Summary statistics were harmonized to HapMap3, excluding non-SNP, strand-ambiguous, duplicate and allele-mismatched records.
Munging used signed effect directions and P values, with INFO ≥ 0.8 and MAF ≥ 0.01 where measured fields were available.
P values stored as zero were replaced by 10 -300 .
Analyses used the European reference LD scores and regression weights distributed with LDSC, with freely estimated intercepts.

The 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated as:
Statistical inflation was described by the LDSC intercept, mean chi-squared statistic and attenuation ratio, calculated as: .
External statistics were standardized to SNP identifier, alleles, signed effect, SE, P value and sample size.
Odds ratios were log-transformed, and signed effect fields were derived from Z statistics when necessary.
LDSC munging used P values and signed effect directions and HapMap3 allele alignment.
Palindromic variants were excluded.
Bivariate LDSC estimated correlations between each BAG/BAU trait and each external phenotype using European LD scores and regression weights 61 .
text.formatted: Bivariate LDSC estimated correlations between each BAG/BAU trait and each external phenotype using European LD scores and regression weights <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61</ref> .

text.text: Intercepts were freely estimated to accommodate correlated errors, including those arising from sample overlap.
Numerical eligibility required finite rg within [-1, 1], positive finite SE, valid P values and positive external heritability where available.
A dataset failing these checks for any target was excluded from the global testing family, leaving 2,276 datasets and 13,656 comparisons.
Two-sided tests of rg = 0 underwent global BH correction across this family.
Exploratory flags identified low heritability precision (Z < 4), rg SE > 0.2, fewer than 200,000 shared SNPs, incomplete autosomal coverage, and reconstructed summary statistics.
text.formatted: Exploratory flags identified low heritability precision (Z < 4), rg SE > 0.2, fewer than 200,000 shared SNPs, incomplete autosomal coverage, and reconstructed summary statistics.

text.text: To assess associations after mutual adjustment, we regressed each external phenotype's genetic component jointly on BAG and BAU derived from the same biomarker source.
Models covered 45 selected phenotypes for each of the three sources.
Three-trait genetic covariance matrices were estimated using the shared-SNP filters, MHC exclusion, free intercepts and 200-block jackknife described for the six-trait analysis.
Variables were standardized by their total genetic variances.
The standardized genetic regression coefficients for BAG and BAU, mutually adjusted for each other, were:
The first equation gives the coefficient for BAG adjusted for BAU; the second gives the coefficient for BAU adjusted for BAG.
Coefficient sampling covariance was JVJ T , where J is the analytic Jacobian with respect to the three genetic variances and three genetic covariances.
SEs were obtained from the coefficient sampling variances, and 95% CIs used estimate ± 1.96 SE.
Two-sided Wald tests were BH-corrected separately across 135 BAG and 135 BAU coefficients.
A pooled correction across all 270 coefficients was used as a sensitivity analysis.
Estimable models containing any phenotype with heritability Z < 4 were exploratory, including all estimable models containing proteomics-derived BAU.
text.formatted: Estimable models containing any phenotype with heritability Z < 4 were exploratory, including all estimable models containing proteomics-derived BAU.

text.text: Tissue and cell-type enrichment MAGMA (v1.08) tested gene associations using the SNP-wise mean model, per-variant sample sizes and the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 European LD reference 31 .
SNPs were mapped to NCBI37.3 protein-coding gene bodies without flanking extensions, excluding genes overlapping the extended MHC.
Significance was assessed using Bonferroni correction across tested genes within each trait.
MAGMA tissue-expression analyses used GTEx v8 data for 54 tissues provided through FUMA 62 .
One-sided gene-property tests assessed whether higher tissue expression predicted stronger gene associations, accounting for gene-gene correlation.
Models adjusted for mean expression across tissues, gene size, gene density and inverse mean minor-allele count, including log-transformed terms for the latter three.
BH correction covered all 324 tests across six traits and 54 tissues.
DEPICT (v1-rel194) evaluated 209 tissue, cell-population and biospecimen categories using GPL570 expression data and MeSH annotations 32 .
QC-passing variants with P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 /6 were clumped using PLINK 63 (r² = 0.1; 500 kb).
text.formatted: QC-passing variants with P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 /6 were clumped using PLINK <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63</ref> (r² = 0.1; 500 kb).

text.text: LD estimates used the 1000 Genomes Phase 1 CEU, GBR and TSI reference.
Loci were defined using DEPICT's precomputed LD intervals at an r 2 threshold of 0.5, extended to gene boundaries and merged.
The MHC region (chromosome 6:25-35 Mb) was excluded.
Enrichment used 500 gene-count-matched permutations and 50 null repetitions to estimate within-trait FDR, with significance defined as DEPICT-reported FDR < 0.05.
text.formatted: Enrichment used 500 gene-count-matched permutations and 50 null repetitions to estimate within-trait FDR, with significance defined as DEPICT-reported FDR < 0.05.

text.text: Primary analyses required at least ten loci and included the four RBT-and NMR-derived traits.
Sensitivity analyses used P ≤ 5 × 10 -8 ; traits with fewer than ten primary loci were additionally examined at P ≤ 10 -5 as exploratory analyses.
We applied gsMap (v1.73.8) 64 to the Mouse Organogenesis Spatiotemporal Transcriptomic Atlas (MOSTA; https://ftp.cngb.org/pub/SciRAID/stomics/STDS0000058/stomics/) 33 .

text.text: Analyses included all six GWASs and 53 sections from 14 . embryos spanning E9.5-E16.5.
Sections were processed independently, excluding undetected genes, unannotated spatial bins and anatomical groups containing fewer than 30 bins.
Following normalization and dimensionality reduction, gsMap integrated gene expression, spatial coordinates and anatomical labels using a graph-attention autoencoder.
Gene specificity scores measured local expression enrichment relative to the section-wide background, using neighbouring bins with similar expression profiles and matching anatomical labels.
Mouse genes were mapped to human homologues, excluding unmapped and mitochondrial genes.
Gene specificity scores were linked to SNPs using gsMap's precomputed SNP-gene mappings.

Spatial enrichment was assessed using weighted stratified LDSC with the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 European reference, GENCODE release 46 gene annotations mapped to GRCh37 (v46lift37) and baseline annotations.
Variants with nonfinite Z statistics or Z2 ≥ max(80, 0.001 × Nmax) were excluded, where Nmax was the maximum per-variant sample size.
One-sided tests used HLA-excluded HapMap3 regression weights, freely estimated intercepts and 200 jackknife blocks.
Bin-level P values were combined within each anatomical label and section using gsMap's equal-weight Cauchy procedure with default outlier filtering.
Global BH correction was applied across all 5,850 section-tissue-trait tests.
To assess the reproducibility of gsMap associations, we compared tissue-association profiles between the two E16.5 embryos.
For each trait and tissue, association scores were calculated as the median section-level -log10(Cauchy P) within each embryo.
Pearson and Spearman correlations were calculated across 28 shared anatomical labels.
Single-cell analyses used Tabula Sapiens v2 with author-provided cell annotations and donor metadata 65 .

text.text: We used the decontXcounts layer, containing decontaminated 10x counts and unchanged Smart-seq counts.
Cells required at least 200 detected genes, and genes required detection in at least 50 cells.
ERCC spike-ins and ambiguous gene symbols were excluded.
Counts were normalized to 10,000 endogenous counts per cell and log1p-transformed.
The retained atlas comprised 1,136,218 cells from 24 donors and 28 tissues.
We used scDRS (v1.0.3) to assess enrichment of trait-associated gene expression in individual cells relative to matched control gene sets 34 .

text.text: For each trait, the top 1,000 genes from complete MAGMA rankings were selected after mapping Entrez identifiers to unambiguous human gene symbols.
Gene sets were then intersected with the expression matrix without replacing absent genes.
MAGMA P values were converted to association Z-score weights using scDRS's gene-set preparation procedure.
Scoring used scDRS's default variance-stabilizing weights and 1,000 control gene sets matched on mean expression and variance.
Analyses adjusted for sequencing assay and log-transformed detected-gene count.
All six traits used the same full-atlas expression background.
BH correction was applied across individual-cell P values separately for each trait.
Group analyses included tissue, tissue-by-original-cell-type, broad-compartment and unified-cell-type categories.

text.text: Groups required at least 50 cells.
For each group, the 95th percentile of normalized scDRS scores was compared with corresponding statistics from the same cells across 1,000 matched control gene sets.
Empirical P values and association Z scores were derived from this control distribution.
Group-level P values were BH-corrected across all six traits separately for tissue (168 tests), tissue-by-original-cell-type (3,042), unified-cell-type (450) and broad-compartment (36)    analyses.
Comparisons of BAG and BAU group scores were descriptive, without formal between-trait testing.
We integrated positional, eQTL and chromatin-interaction mapping, MAGMA gene associations and multi-SNP summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR-multi).
FUMA positional mapping used a 10-kb window, whereas eQTL mapping applied resource-specific significance thresholds.
Chromatin interactions required FDR ≤ 10 -6 , with promoters defined from 250 bp upstream to 500 bp downstream of transcription start sites.

Overall, these findings support BAU as a new dimension of aging assessment, distinct from but complementary to BAG.
This study has several limitations.

First, BAU was parameterized as the log predictive variance under a Gaussian distribution, whereas alternative or non-parametric formulations may capture asymmetric or heavy-tailed uncertainty differently.

Nevertheless, the strong associations observed across health outcomes, cross-omic profiles, and genetic architectures demonstrate that even a Gaussian-based representation captures biologically informative signals beyond BAG, indicating that the core concept of BAU is robust to distributional assumptions.
Second, as a model-derived metric, BAU inevitably retains residual technical and modeling noise alongside biologically meaningful variation.

However, measured technical and other factors accounted for only a modest proportion of BAU variance, and individual BAU rankings remained highly consistent following rigorous adjustment and across alternative model specifications.
Third, the primary NMR and proteomic models were trained and evaluated within the UK Biobank, requiring further testing in external cohorts with harmonized omics depth.

Nonetheless, RBT-derived BAU remained independently predictive of mortality across three external validation cohorts without cohort-specific re-fitting or recalibration, supporting the broader generalizability of this framework across diverse populations.This study also has several strengths.

First, to our knowledge, this work provides the first population-scale characterization of BAU as an essential dimension of human aging, spanning longitudinal health outcomes, multi-omic profiling, and genome-wide genetic analyses.

By jointly modeling central tendency and dispersion, our probabilistic framework moves beyond single scalar age estimates to represent biological age as a distribution, simultaneously quantifying BAG and BAU.
Second, BAU demonstrated clear clinical utility by providing predictive information beyond BAG across mortality, healthspan loss, multimorbidity, and diverse incident diseases.

Importantly, both baseline BAU and its longitudinal change independently tracked future health decline, while RBT-derived BAU successfully generalized across independent populations, highlighting its potential for individualized risk . stratification and clinical monitoring.
Third, integrated multi-omic and genetic analyses established distinct biological foundations for BAU and BAG, disentangling the biology of BAU from that of BAG.

Together, cross-omic signal divergence alongside specific immune, metabolic, and tissue-remodeling signatures establishes discordant aging as a hallmark of high BAU.In conclusion, our findings redefine biological age as a probabilistic state characterized jointly by its position and its uncertainty.
BAG quantifies the position of an inferred age state from chronological age, whereas BAU measures how broadly biological signals disperse across compatible age states.
Comprehensive evidence from prospective health outcomes, multi-omic profiles, and genetic analyses establishes BAU as an independent and essential dimension of human biological aging beyond BAG.
Individual variation in aging thus spans two distinct axes, the position of an age state and the degree of discordant aging across biological systems.

A distributional representation of biological age therefore provides a comprehensive framework for understanding aging heterogeneity and evaluating individual vulnerability to future health decline. .
